passage:
Deepak, you look nervous about tomorrow, so let me tell you my story. I'm Chinmay. At twenty-five they made me team lead over Sunil, Farida and Bhaskar, my friends from the first day. The first feedback I ever gave was to Sunil. I was so afraid of hurting him that I said, “It's nearly perfect,” and the report went out with an error. The next month, panicking, I over-corrected. I sent Farida a long, sharp email about her mistake, copying everyone. She didn't speak to me for a week.

Then Sunil told me over tea, “We don't need you soft or harsh. Just straight.” So I started giving feedback in private, early, with one thing that was good and one thing to change. It felt awkward for months. It got easier.

qa.q: Who received the first feedback Chinmay ever gave?
qa.a: The first feedback Chinmay ever gave was to Sunil.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay say, “It's nearly perfect”?
qa.a: Chinmay was afraid of hurting Sunil, so softening the truth felt safer than being straight.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change after Sunil's words over tea?
qa.a: Chinmay began giving feedback in private and early, with one good thing and one thing to change.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt receiving a long, sharp email copied to everyone?
qa.a: Farida probably felt humiliated and angry, exposed in front of everyone, which fits the week of silence.

grounding: An elder recalls becoming team lead of former friends, being too soft and then too harsh with feedback before finding a steady, respectful tone.

passage:
The client deck was due in two hours and the shared printer had jammed. Anjali, three weeks into managing her old college friends, looked at Kalyani's slides and winced. The numbers on slide four were wrong. “It's fine,” Anjali said quickly, then, “Well, mostly fine.” Kalyani's smile faded. “What does that mean?”

Anjali's face went warm. She took a breath. “Slide four has last quarter's numbers. I should have said so right away. Can we fix it together? I'll read the numbers, you type.” Kalyani nodded, a little stiffly. Twenty minutes later the slide was right.

“Thanks for telling me straight,” Kalyani said quietly, “instead of saying fine.”

qa.q: What was wrong on slide four?
qa.a: Slide four had last quarter's numbers.

qa.q: Why did Anjali say “It's fine” first?
qa.a: Anjali felt awkward correcting a friend and reached for softness before finding a straight tone.

qa.q: What did Anjali suggest to fix the slide?
qa.a: Anjali suggested reading out the numbers while Kalyani typed.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt on first hearing “Well, mostly fine”?
qa.a: Kalyani probably felt worried and unsure what was wrong, as the fading smile suggests.

grounding: A young manager of former friends feels awkward giving feedback, is too soft at first and then finds a steady, respectful tone.

passage:
Monday
First week as team lead. Ira and I sat together for two years. We went for chaat every Friday.
Today I had to tell her that her reports keep missing the client's numbers. I said, “It's totally fine, don't worry, maybe just check once?” She laughed and said, “Sure, boss.” Nothing will change. I was too soft.
Wednesday
The report was wrong again. I snapped at her in front of everyone. “Ira, this is the third time!” Her face went red. I felt horrible.
Friday
I asked her for chaat. I apologised for Wednesday. Then I said, calmly, “I need the client numbers checked every time. Can we make a checklist together?” She nodded. We did.
Minakshi

qa.q: What did Ira and Minakshi do every Friday?
qa.a: They went for chaat every Friday.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel after snapping on Wednesday?
qa.a: Minakshi felt horrible and embarrassed after being harsh in front of everyone.

qa.q: What worked on Friday, and why?
qa.a: Apologising, then stating the need clearly and calmly and offering a checklist together, found a steady, respectful tone.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt when Minakshi snapped in front of everyone?
qa.a: She likely felt humiliated and hurt, her face going red, especially from a friend.

grounding: A young manager writes about giving feedback to a former peer, first too soft, then too harsh, before finding a steady, respectful tone.

passage:
At the garment unit in Ludhiana's outskirts, Rehana had been promoted to line supervisor over the women she'd sewn beside for three years.
Jasleen, her closest friend on the line, kept arriving late. For two weeks, Rehana said nothing. The others noticed. “Supervisor's friend can do anything,” someone muttered.
Then, on Monday, Rehana lost her temper and shouted at Jasleen in front of the whole floor. Jasleen went silent for two days.
On Wednesday, Rehana waited for her at the gate. “I was wrong to shout. And I was wrong to say nothing before. I need you on time, like everyone. What's making you late?”
Jasleen sighed. “My son's school bus changed.” They worked out a new shift together.

qa.q: How long had Rehana sewn beside the women?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when someone muttered about the supervisor's friend?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and uneasy, knowing her silence looked like favouritism.

qa.q: What did Rehana do on Wednesday that worked?
qa.a: She apologised for both extremes, stated the need clearly, and asked what was causing the lateness, finding a steady, fair tone.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt when Rehana shouted in front of the floor?
qa.a: She likely felt humiliated and hurt, which is why she went silent for two days.

grounding: Shows a newly promoted supervisor with a friend on her team swinging from too soft to too harsh before finding a steady, respectful tone.

passage:
When Sofia became shift manager at the bakery in Toronto, the first thing that changed was the break room. Kaito, who'd split pastries with her for two years, stopped mid-joke when she walked in. Maya started calling her "boss", half teasing.
That first week Kaito kept arriving twenty minutes late. Sofia said nothing, then said, "No worries!", then covered his station herself. By Friday she snapped at him in front of the morning crew: "Third time. Do you even care?" The kitchen went silent. Kaito's ears turned red.
That night she couldn't sleep.
On Monday she asked him to step out back. "I handled Friday badly. I'm sorry I did that in front of everyone. And I still need you here at six. Is something making mornings hard?"
Kaito rubbed his neck. "The new bus route. I'll get the earlier one."
They both breathed out.

qa.q: How late did Kaito keep arriving?
qa.a: Twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling the night after snapping at Kaito?
qa.a: Sofia felt guilty and restless, unable to sleep, knowing she had swung from too soft to too harsh.

qa.q: What made Sofia's Monday conversation steadier?
qa.a: She apologised for the public telling-off, kept the expectation clear, and asked what was making mornings hard.

qa.q: What was Friday like for Kaito?
qa.a: Kaito felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears turning red as a friend scolded him in front of the whole crew.

grounding: Shows a young manager supervising a former peer, first too soft and then too harsh, before finding a steady, respectful tone.
